headline: Japan Crosses 100,000 Centenarians, Revealing Secrets to Long Life
meta_description: Japan now has 107,677 people aged 100 or older—more than any country. Diet, daily movement, and assistive technology reveal what's behind this historic milesto…
summary_short: Japan has reached a historic milestone: 107,677 centenarians, the most of any nation. Here's what their lives reveal about aging well.
body:
Japan has crossed a historic threshold with 107,677 people now aged 100 or older—the first time the country has surpassed 100,000 centenarians and more than any nation on Earth. The milestone reflects decades of progress: when Japan began tracking centenarians in 1963, only 153 people qualified. By 1981 the count had reached 1,000; by 1998, it had grown to 10,000. Today, the curve continues to accelerate. Among these remarkable elders, eighty-eight percent are women. The oldest is Kishimoto Fuyo, 114, from Kyoto City, while the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, 112, from Kumamoto. Every year on Japan's "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, those turning 100 receive a personal letter and a traditional sake cup from the prime minister—and this year, that meant many more letters to send.

The factors behind this longevity are surprisingly straightforward. Japanese diet emphasizes fish, vegetables, and rice with significantly less saturated fat than typical Western food. Movement matters equally: older Japanese tend to stay physically active not through structured exercise, but through daily habits sustained over decades—walking, cycling, using public transit, and stretching. Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno also credits "progress in medicine and technology," noting that Japanese companies have developed assistive technologies that help older people with mobility and vision challenges remain independent longer.

Yet this celebration masks a profound demographic crisis. Japan's fertility rate has plummeted to 1.14 children per woman—below the 2.1 needed for population replacement. By 2070, Japan's population is projected to fall roughly 30 percent, to 87 million people, with those aged 65 and older representing nearly 40 percent of the population. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called the decline a "quiet emergency." This creates an unsustainable equation: more pensioners and care recipients, fewer working-age people paying taxes to support them. Government programs aimed at raising birth rates have failed to shift the trajectory, leaving Japan facing an urgent challenge even as it celebrates its centenarians.
quick_facts: Japan now has 107,677 people aged 100 or older—more than any other country
Kishimoto Fuyo, 114, from Kyoto City, is Japan's oldest living person
Japanese diet features fish, vegetables, and rice with less saturated fat
The centenarian count grew from 153 in 1963 to over 100,000 today
Japan's fertility rate hit record low of 1.14 children per woman
